title: The long way to work
text: The commute was the great fixed cost of city life, and the pandemic {{1}} it. For a century, workers had {{2}} the trip — an hour each way, five days a week — in {{3}} for the wage and the city. Remote work did not abolish the journey; it made it {{4}}. Some commutes have turned into {{5}}: a walk that replaces the morning scroll, a train carriage that is the only hour of the day nobody can {{6}}. Employers, meanwhile, discovered that the office commute was a {{7}} of commitment — visible, costly and, to their surprise, resented accordingly. Cities are adjusting: rail operators have {{8}} flexible season tickets, and planners talk about the fifteen-minute city, where daily needs sit within a short walk. The commute is not dying. It is being renegotiated, like everything else that used to be compulsory.

gaps.explanation: 'the pandemic shook it' — rattled but did not destroy it; shoo = wave away, shrill = make a piercing sound.
'workers had endured the trip' — suffered it patiently; entice = tempt, entrench = fix firmly.
'in return for the wage' — the fixed phrase; ransom = money demanded for a release.
'it made it optional' — no longer required; obligatory means the exact opposite.
'turned into rituals: a walk that replaces the morning scroll' — ceremonies of daily life; recital = a performance from memory.
'the only hour nobody can interrupt' — break into it; intercept = stop something in transit.
'the commute was a display of commitment' — a visible showing of it; doctrine = a set of beliefs.
'operators have introduced flexible season tickets' — brought them into use; instil = plant gradually in the mind.
